newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sexual harassment insurance to go on sale in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Sexual harassment insurance to go on sale in Japan.

text.p: Japanese companies, often criticised for ignorance of sexual harassment, will soon be able to take out insurance against claims from aggrieved workers, the firm offering the new service said on Wednesday.

AIU Insurance Co, a Japanese unit of American International Group Inc, said it would be the first such product in the Japanese market allowing companies to protect themselves against claims for sexual harassment.
The firm's belief that a viable market for such insurance exists in Japan is a sign that the issue is finally starting to get Japanese companies' attention.

"We have acquired the first licence in Japan to sell a policy which insures a company, and its foreign subsidiaries, against claims of sexual harassment, and we will be selling it from April 1," AIU said in a statement.

"The internationalisation of Japanese companies continues, particularly with companies entering the United States, where Japanese companies already have around 500,000 non-Japanese employees," the statement added.

"Suits filed by employees against Japanese companies for discrimination, wrongful dismissal and sexual harassment are on the rise. In this context, the company has received many inquiries about ways to safeguard against the possibility of...these kind of prosecutions and damages cases."
The licence was issued by Japan's Ministry of Finance, which confirmed AIU was the first company to approach it about selling sexual harassment insurance to companies in Japan.
AIU has about 50 percent of Japan's so-called "third-sector" insurance business, which deals with personal accident, health and other niche insurance products.
Sexual harassment -- called "sekuhara" in Japanese -- was long ignored by most Japanese companies but in the past year high-profile cases have started to change attitudes.

In the United States, Japan's Mitsubishi Motors Corp is being sued by female workers at its Normal, Illinois, plant who allege many female employees were subjected to sexual harassment that the company did nothing to address.

Last November, in the first successful suit against sex discrimination in promotion, the Tokyo District Court awarded 12 female bank employees of Tokyo's Shiba Credit Association a total of 100 million yen ($806,000) in compensation and ordered the company to promote them.
Media reports estimate that Japanese courts at present are considering about 25 sexual harassment claims.
AIU declined to give details on a typical premium or estimates of the potential value of the business in Japan.
AIU spokesman Kenji Yamashita told Reuters that insurance protection would not be offered unless the firm asking for it agreed to carry out a sexual harassment education programme.

"The condition is that the policy holder educates all employees about sekuhara. For example, in companies where there are nude posters stuck up on the walls, they need to be told what is right and what is wrong," he said.
He said companies should not stop addressing the issue just because they took out insurance.
"The policy doesn't cover sekuhara if the people doing it are aware of what they're doing, such as linking promotion to going out with the boss," he said. ($1=124 yen)
